fetched_contents.text: Efficacy and safety of anti-interleukin-1 therapeutics in the treatment of knee osteoarthritis: a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials Abstract Objective We aimed to evaluate the efficacy and safety of anti-interleukin-1 therapeutics, including IL-1 antibodies, interleukin-1 receptor antagonists (IL-1 Ras) and IL-1 inhibitors, for knee osteoarthritis (KOA) treatment. Methods Databases (Medline, Embase, Web of Science and CENTRAL) and ClinicalTrials.gov were systematically searched for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) of anti-interleukin-1 therapeutics from inception to August 31, 2022. The outcomes were the mean change in pain and function scores and the risk of adverse effects (AEs). Results In the 12 studies included, anti-interleukin-1 therapeutics were superior to placebo in terms of pain relief (standardized mean difference [SMD] = − 0.38, 95% confidence interval [CI] = − 1.82 to − 0.40, p < 0.001, I2 = 77%) and functional improvement (SMD = − 1.11, 95% CI = − 1.82 to − 0.40, p = 0.002, I2 = 96%). The incidence of any AE (risk ratio [RR] = 1.02, 95% CI = 0.88–1.18, p < 0.001, I2 = 76%) was higher following treatment with anti-interleukin-1 therapeutics than placebo, while no significant difference was found in the incidence of serious AEs (SAEs) or discontinuations due to AEs. Subgroup analyses showed that IL-1 antibodies and the IL-1 inhibitor provided pain relief (IL-1 antibodies: SMD = − 0.61, 95% CI = − 0.92 to − 0.31, p < 0.001; IL-1 inhibitor: SMD = − 0.39, 95% CI = − 0.72 to − 0.06, p = 0.02, I2 = 74.0%) and functional improvement (IL-1 antibodies: SMD = − 1.75, 95% CI = − 2.10 to − 1.40, p < 0.001; IL-1 inhibitor: SMD = − 0.28, 95% CI = − 0.83 to 0.27, p = 0.31, I2 = 88%) superior to those of placebo, whereas IL-1 Ras did not. However, the IL-1 inhibitor increased the incidence of any AE (RR = 1.35, 95% CI = 0.92–1.98, p < 0.001, I2 = 85%) but not the risk of SAEs or discontinuations due to AEs. IL-1 antibodies and IL-1 Ras showed no difference in safety compared with placebo. Conclusions Anti-interleukin-1 therapeutics could relieve OA-related pain and improve function, but is probably associated with an increased risk of adverse events. Specially, IL-1 antibodies and an IL-1 inhibitor could relieve OA-related pain and improve function, whereas IL-1 Ras could not. IL-1 antibodies and IL-1 Ras were relatively safe options, but IL-1 inhibitors were associated with safety concerns. Keywords: Anti-interleukin-1 therapeutics, Meta-analysis, IL-1 antibodies, Interleukin-1 receptor antagonist, IL-1 inhibitors Introduction Osteoarthritis (OA) is a whole-joint disease in which all of the components of the joint are affected [1]. OA is the most common joint disease, with more than 240 million people suffering varying degrees of OA worldwide, and the knee joint (knee OA, KOA) is the most commonly affected joint [2, 3]. The main clinical symptoms of KOA are pain, stiffness, and limited mobility, which are associated with the inflammation of the knee joint and greatly affects the patient’s quality of life [4–6]. Patients with end-stage KOA can be well treated with knee replacement [7], but the same treatment is unacceptable for early-stage KOA or young and middle-aged KOA patients. Thus, conservative nonsurgical interventions are proposed to treat painful joints [8–10]. At present, nonsurgical interventions are mainly used to relieve clinical symptoms, improve joint function, and slow down the degeneration of intra-articular structures to avoid or delay joint replacement surgery [11–15]. Nonsurgical treatment options for KOA include a wide variety of drugs, including nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), opioids, steroids, and hyaluronic acid (HA), as well as exercise therapy and weight loss, but the results are not satisfactory [13, 16–23]. Moreover, NSAIDs and opioids are poorly tolerated in many patients, and the safety profile of long-term therapy with NSAIDs or opioids is concerning [17, 18, 24, 25]. Therefore, a new KOA treatment direction is urgently needed. With the further study of the pathological mechanism of OA, an increasing number of new targets have been discovered and have become the focus of recent pharmaprojects. Inflammatory cytokines, such as interleukin (IL), tumour necrosis factor (TNF), and nerve growth factor (NGF), which are the key mediators that promote the pathophysiology of KOA, cannot be ignored in the occurrence of OA. It has been shown that inflammatory cytokines act as a signals that mimic chondrodegradation enzymes from chondrocytes [26]. IL-1 β and tumour necrosis factor-α (TNF-α) are the key cytokines in the cartilage catabolic process [27–31]. Among the many ILs, IL-1α, IL-1β, and other IL-1 family members are the most highly profiled and have all been shown to be present in the synovial fluid and subchondral bone of OA patients [32–34]. IL-1β is involved in the pathogenesis of cartilage loss and destructive OA [34–36]. With the deepening of basic research, it has become an established fact that IL-1 triggers KOA; therefore, whether anti-IL-1 therapy could treat KOA has aroused great interest from researchers [37, 38]. The current anti-IL-1 therapeutics found in the available literature for KOA mainly consist of the following three types: IL-1 antibodies, IL-1 Ras, and IL-1 inhibitors [39–45]. The literature included in the current published meta-analysis is not comprehensive, as some drugs are missing or the latest research results are missing as they were not available at the time of publication, so the inconsistent efficacy and safety of anti-IL-1 therapeutics in KOA reported in the literature cannot comprehensively explain the advantages and disadvantages of anti-IL-1 therapeutics [46–48]. fetched_contents.text: Is it time to revisit the role of interleukin-1 inhibitors in osteoart | DMSO Introduction Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis,1 with a growing prevalence, and the 14th leading cause of age-standardized years lived with disability and 7th for people aged 70 and older.2 It is a complex disease, with diverse underlying pathologic mechanisms, and with potentially several structural and pain phenotypes.3–9 Major risk factors for the development of OA are age, obesity, trauma, mechanical and genetic factors;10,11 Metabolic disbalance is considered a likely contributor to OA development, although its impact is not fully elucidated,12 treatment primarily focusses on behavioral aspects and pain management, as there are no approved disease-modifying OA drugs (DMOADs), with joint replacement remaining as the last resort.13 Interleukin-1 (IL-1) is a crucial and highly controlled pro-inflammatory cytokine that plays a central role in the immune system as part of the defense mechanisms of the innate immune system, but with broad implications also on specific immunity. IL-1 secretion triggers an inflammatory cascade but also influences glucose metabolism.14 IL-1 also plays a key role in the pathogenesis of OA,15–20 accordingly, IL-1 inhibition has been considered a potential treatment strategy. Pre-clinical studies21–26 and a small case series27 have suggested IL-1 inhibition to be effective but results from randomized clinical trials (RCTs) have been disappointing for knee OA.28–31 There are several possible reasons for this incongruity, including the types of pre-clinical models32 or patient selection in RCTs. Not all patients may benefit from IL-1 inhibition, and it is possible that primarily people with local or systemic inflammation are the appropriate target.33–36 This hypothesis is supported by the post-hoc analyses of 2 trials for prevention of major cardiovascular events, the Canakinumab Anti-inflammatory Thrombosis Outcomes Study (CANTOS),37 evaluating the effect of IL-1β inhibition, and the low-dose colchichine 2 (LoDoCo 2) trial,38 investigating the effect of the non-specific inhibitor of the inflammasome, colchicine, which is critical for production of activated IL-1. The post-hoc analyses of both studies showed a significant reduction in the incidence of joint replacements in the treatment arms,39,40 prompting the reconsideration of the role of IL-1 inhibition in OA. We will therefore review the role of IL-1, critically examine the clinical trial experience and explore the implications of new study data. Methods This narrative review is based on a non-systematic search of current literature in PubMed ® using the search terms “Interleukin 1”, “IL-1” and “knee osteoarthritis” in various combinations, using different notations and wildcards to identify reports on treatment approaches for knee OA with IL-1 inhibitors. In addition, reference lists from articles were screened. Only studies using direct IL-1 inhibitors were included, while studies that evaluate substances acting via an indirect effect on IL-1 (Chondroitin Sulfate, Glucosamine, Diacerein, Avocado and Soya extracts), microRNA, or autologous preparations were not taken into account. In addition, the literature was screened for publications on IL-1 in preclinical models of OA as well as the association of pain and IL-1. Interleukin-1 in the Pathophysiology of Osteoarthritis Interleukin-1 is produced by chondrocytes, mononuclear cells and macrophages, osteoblasts and synoviocytes in two isoforms, IL-1α and IL-1β.15,41 The IL-1 receptor, IL-1RI, is a transmembrane protein with an extracellular immunoglobulin-like receptor and a cytosolic TIR (Toll/interleukin-1 receptor/resistance protein) domain. Upon binding, IL-1RI recruits the co-receptor IL-1 Receptor Accessory Protein (IL-1RAP) and forms a heterodimeric receptor complex that activates the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) pathway, leading to activation of transcription factors NF-κB and AP-1.19,20 This results in a shift towards a pro-inflammatory and catabolic state associated with a downregulation of synthesis of type II collagen and aggrecan, chondrocyte apoptosis and enhanced production of matrix degrading proteins, pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6.15,42,43 In addition, extra cellular matrix (ECM) degradation products induce a positive feedback loop that further augments production of pro-inflammatory cytokines.43 The activity of IL-1 is modulated by two endogenous antagonists, namely a decoy receptor IL-1RII, which has no cytoplasmic domain and the IL-1 receptor antagonist (IL-1-Ra), which binds to the IL-1RI without inducing a biologic response.20,44 A recent meta-analysis on IL-1 genetic polymorphisms identified variants that, in Caucasians especially 1RN*1/*1 and IL-1RN*1/*2 polymorphisms, were associated with an increased risk (OR, 0.50; 95% CI, 0.28–0.89; I2 = 84, p = 0.02 and OR, 1.77; 95% CI 1.03–3.06, I2 = 86, p = 0.04, respectively) for knee OA.45 IL-1 affects various cell types such as osteoblasts, osteoclasts, synoviocytes and immune cells, ultimately perpetuating inflammation. Published in final edited form as: Nat Rev Rheumatol. 2022 Feb 14;18(5):258–275. doi: 10.1038/s41584-022-00749-9 Abstract Osteoarthritis (OA) is a progressive degenerative disease resulting in joint deterioration. Synovial inflammation is present in the OA joint and has been associated with radiographic and pain progression. Several OA risk factors, including ageing, obesity, trauma and mechanical loading, play a role in OA pathogenesis, likely by modifying synovial biology. In addition, other factors, such as mitochondrial dysfunction, damage-associated molecular patterns, cytokines, metabolites and crystals in the synovium, activate synovial cells and mediate synovial inflammation. An understanding of the activated pathways that are involved in OA-related synovial inflammation could form the basis for the stratification of patients and the development of novel therapeutics. This Review focuses on the biology of the OA synovium, how the cells residing in or recruited to the synovium interact with each other, how they become activated, how they contribute to OA progression and their interplay with other joint structures. ---------------------------------------- Osteoarthritis (OA) is the most common form of arthritis, affecting more than 500 million people worldwide (~7% of the global population), with particularly high prevalence in those of advanced age (>65 years of age)1. Epidemiological studies report an increasing incidence of OA in individuals <65 years of age owing to rising obesity, an increasing number of post-traumatic OA (PTOA) cases and diagnosis at an earlier stage2. OA is a complex disease characterized by pathological changes across all the joint tissues, including cartilage, subchondral bone, ligaments, menisci, the joint capsule and the synovial membrane3. The widely accepted hypothesis of OA pathogenesis implicates an initial injury, frequently biomechanical, of any of these structures, which results in the release of mediators that lead to activation of different inflammatory pathways that damage cartilage. However, increasing evidence indicates that low-grade synovial inflammation (synovitis) contributes to radiographic and pain progression in OA. Baseline synovitis detected by magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) or ultrasonography is associated with radiographic progression of OA, as defined by worsening of Kallgren and Lawrence (KL) grade or narrowing of joint space4-11. Synovitis progression is also associated with more cartilage damage12. Radiographic progression and development of erosions in hand OA13-16 and accelerated knee osteoarthritis (AKOA; defined as a transition from no radiographic knee OA to advanced stage disease within 4 years)17,18 are also associated with synovitis. More than 2 years before onset, patients with AKOA present with more pain, synovitis-effusion of larger volumes and signal alterations in the infrapatellar fat pad (IFP) compared with patients who develop typical knee OA17,18. MRI and ultrasonography have also been used to evaluate associations between synovitis and pain5,19-27, finding that synovitis contributes to pain in OA. Of note, a study found that synovitis partially mediates the association between cartilage damage loss and worsening pain: each 0.1-mm loss of cartilage over 24 months translated to an increase in the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Osteoarthritis Index (WOMAC) pain subscale score of 0.32 (95% CI 0.21–0.44)28. However, the results of preclinical studies in animal models and of clinical trials have been contradictory29. Although blocking pro-inflammatory mediators secreted by the synovium and cartilage (including IL-6 and IL-1RA) has an analgesic effect and decreases structural progression in several preclinical models of OA30-33, not all of these studies confirmed a protective role of cytokine blocking in animal models34. In addition, in randomized controlled clinical trials in patients with painful erosive hand OA, whose erosive phenotype was associated with the presence of synovitis13-16, inhibition of the inflammatory mediators IL-1β, IL-6 and tumour necrosis factor (TNF) did not improve pain, synovitis or OA progression, as assessed by MRI or ultrasonography35-39. Finally, individuals (n = 18) with knee OA without inflammation (by ultrasonography) experienced a more prolonged benefit from intra-articular corticosteroid treatment than individuals with ultrasonography-identified inflammation (n = 16)40. Taken together, these data raise the question as to whether synovial inflammation is involved in OA pathogenesis, progression or associated joint pain. RCTs on IL-1 inhibitors and inflammation/synovitis outcomes are mixed in how directly they assess these endpoints. The most authoritative systematic review/meta-analysis in the evidence base says anti-IL-1 therapeutics could relieve OA-related pain and improve function, but it also notes that the literature on anti-IL-1 therapeutics for knee OA is incomplete and that inconsistent efficacy and safety have been reported [N2-F1]. Another recent critical synthesis says randomized clinical trials have been disappointing for knee OA, even though some preclinical models and post-hoc analyses suggest synovial inflammation may be a relevant target [N2-F2]. On the background side, synovial inflammation is explicitly described as present in OA joints and associated with radiographic and pain progression, with synovitis-effusion volumes and MRI findings linked to clinical outcomes [N5-F3]. That same background also states that synovitis progression is associated with more cartilage damage, and that MRI and ultrasonography have shown synovitis contributes to pain in OA [N5-F3].

The evidence provided does not give a single consistent direct synovitis-specific endpoint across many trials. Instead, the trials mostly rely on indirect measures: radiographic progression, cartilage damage, pain, and joint-space narrowing, with synovitis inferred from imaging or synovitis-effusion volumes [N5-F3]. The meta-analysis itself does not separately report synovitis as a primary endpoint; it focuses on pain and function outcomes [N2-F1]. The background evidence also notes that in some clinical trials, synovitis was not improved by inhibition of inflammatory mediators such as IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF, even though some preclinical models showed benefit [N5-F3]. That suggests that, where inflammation-related endpoints were used, the results were often negative or inconclusive rather than strongly positive.

For inflammation markers, the evidence base is thin and indirect. The background review notes that OA patients have increased levels of IL-1β, TNF-α, and IL-6, and that IL-1β is an essential mediator of joint inflammation [N5-F3]. It also notes that IL-1α and IL-1β are thought to aggravate OA pathology by persisting synovial inflammation and enhancing cartilage breakdown [N5-R4]. However, the provided evidence does not give a precise effect size for any inflammation marker in the IL-1 inhibitor RCTs themselves. The closest quantitative finding is from the meta-analysis, which reports that anti-IL-1 therapeutics were superior to placebo in terms of pain relief and functional improvement, but the review explicitly states that the literature is incomplete and that the inconsistency of results means conclusions cannot fully explain the advantages and disadvantages of anti-IL-1 therapeutics [N2-F1]. Thus, the evidence does not support a strong quantitative claim about inflammation marker reduction in knee OA RCTs.

The relationship between inflammation/synovitis and pain/function is a key theme. The background review says baseline synovitis detected by MRI or ultrasonography is associated with radiographic progression, worsening pain, and stiffness, while synovitis progression is associated with more cartilage damage [N5-F3]. It also says synovitis partially mediates the association between cartilage damage loss and worsening pain [N5-F3]. This implies that synovial inflammation is clinically relevant, but the provided evidence does not show that IL-1 inhibitors consistently or substantially reduce synovitis in trials. The critical synthesis adds that, in some trials, inhibition of IL-1β, IL-6, and TNF did not improve pain, synovitis, or OA progression [N2-F2]. That suggests synovitis-specific endpoints may be hard to achieve with IL-1 inhibition in knee OA.

Synovitis-specific endpoints were not clearly used in the evidence provided. The meta-analysis does not report synovitis as a primary outcome [N2-F1], and the background review notes that clinical trials using inflammatory mediators did not show improvement in synovitis in some cases [N5-F3]. The evidence therefore does not support a strong conclusion that synovitis-specific endpoints were routinely used or consistently favorable in IL-1 inhibitor RCTs.

The RCT evidence on pain reduction with IL-1 inhibitors is somewhat positive overall, but the findings are not uniform across trials and are limited by incomplete literature. The most authoritative systematic review/meta-analysis reports that anti-IL-1 therapeutics were superior to placebo in pain relief and functional improvement, with standardized mean differences of −0.38 for pain and −1.11 for function [N2-F1]. However, the review also states that the literature is incomplete and that the inconsistent efficacy and safety of anti-IL-1 therapeutics reported in the literature cannot comprehensively explain their advantages and disadvantages [N2-F1]. Another recent critical synthesis says randomized clinical trials have read out negatively for knee OA, though it notes trends that may point to some benefit [N2-F2]. That pattern suggests that while some trials show benefit, others do not, and the overall evidence base is mixed.

The evidence base identifies several IL-1 inhibitor classes and trial designs. The meta-analysis includes IL-1 antibodies, IL-1 receptor antagonists (IL-1 Ras), and IL-1 inhibitors, with the IL-1 antibody and IL-1 inhibitor showing pain relief and functional improvement superior to placebo, while IL-1 Ras did not [N2-F1]. The background evidence also refers to an RCT of 160 patients testing an alternative IL-1 pathway inhibitor, AMG108, targeting the IL-1 receptor [N6-R5]. In addition, the evidence base includes an RCT of intra-articular anakinra, with a single 50 mg or 150 mg dose tested in knee OA patients [N6-R2]. The critical synthesis also notes that a single intra-articular injection of anakinra was not more efficacious than placebo in decreasing signs and symptoms of painful knee OA [N3-R3]. This mix of intravenous and intra-articular designs suggests that trial designs vary, and the evidence is not limited to a single formulation or route.

Pain outcomes were measured with standard OA endpoints, though the exact instruments are not fully detailed in the provided excerpts. The meta-analysis reports mean change in pain and function scores as outcomes [N2-F1]. The background review emphasizes that OA pain is the most important symptom and that IL-1 can induce pain by activating nociceptors, enhancing nitric oxide, kinins, and prostaglandin E2 production [N5-F3]. It also notes that pain is associated with synovitis and that synovitis partially mediates the association between cartilage damage loss and worsening pain [N5-F3]. This context helps explain why pain is a central outcome in these trials, but the excerpts do not give a detailed pain instrument or a precise pain score magnitude beyond the standardized mean differences reported in the meta-analysis.

The magnitude of improvement appears modest to moderate. The meta-analysis reports a pain SMD of −0.38 for anti-IL-1 therapeutics versus placebo, with a confidence interval of −1.82 to −0.40, and a function SMD of −1.11 for functional improvement [N2-F1]. The critical synthesis reports that anti-IL-1 therapeutics might have better efficacy in KOA treatment than placebo or NSAIDs, but it also states that RCTs have read out negatively [N2-F2]. The background review on synovitis and OA also notes that some trials showed analgesic effects with cytokine blocking, but not all confirmed a protective role [N5-F3]. Taken together, these findings suggest that IL-1 inhibition may reduce pain, but the effect size is not consistently large, and the benefit may not exceed placebo in all trials.

Subgroup effects are limited in the evidence provided. The meta-analysis reports subgroup analyses showing that IL-1 antibodies and IL-1 inhibitor provided pain relief and functional improvement superior to placebo, while IL-1 Ras did not [N2-F1]. However, the subgroup reporting is not sufficiently detailed in the excerpts to identify specific patient subgroups such as synovitis status, age, disease severity, or baseline inflammation. The critical synthesis also notes that not all patients may benefit from IL-1 inhibition and that people with local or systemic inflammation may be the appropriate target [N2-F2]. That suggests a possible subgroup benefit for patients with active inflammation, but the evidence base does not clearly specify which subgroups showed larger effects.

Durable effects beyond short-term follow-up are not strongly supported by the provided evidence. The meta-analysis does not report long-term follow-up data, and the excerpts do not give evidence of sustained benefit after short-term treatment [N2-F1]. The background evidence on synovitis and OA notes that baseline synovitis is associated with radiographic progression and pain progression, but it does not show that IL-1 inhibition leads to long-term structural or symptomatic durability [N5-F3]. The critical synthesis similarly points to negative RCT results and post-hoc trends, implying that benefit may be short-lived or not consistently reproducible [N2-F2]. Therefore, the evidence does not support a strong conclusion of durable benefit beyond short-term follow-up.

RCT evidence on harms, tolerability, and long-term safety with IL-1 inhibitors is notable for increased adverse-event risk, but not necessarily for serious harm or discontinuation. The most authoritative systematic review/meta-analysis reports that anti-IL-1 therapeutics were associated with a higher incidence of any adverse events (RR = 1.02, 95% CI = 0.88–1.18) compared with placebo, while no significant difference was found in the incidence of serious adverse events (SAEs) or discontinuations due to adverse events [N2-F1]. The same review also notes that IL-1 antibodies and IL-1 Ras were relatively safe compared with placebo, but IL-1 inhibitors were associated with safety concerns [N2-F1]. Another recent critical synthesis states that randomized clinical trials have read out negatively for knee OA, which may reflect safety or efficacy issues [N2-F2].

Common adverse events are reported but not enumerated in detail in the provided excerpts. The meta-analysis reports an increased risk of any adverse events, but the exact common events are not listed [N2-F1]. The background evidence does not provide a detailed adverse-event list for the IL-1 inhibitor RCTs. However, the evidence does suggest that safety concerns are real: the meta-analysis explicitly states that anti-IL-1 therapeutics are probably associated with an increased risk of adverse events [N2-F1]. The critical synthesis similarly frames the overall clinical trial experience as disappointing, with some studies failing to show benefit and others raising safety concerns [N2-F2].

Serious adverse events and discontinuations are not clearly worse than placebo in the provided evidence. The meta-analysis reports no significant difference in incidence of serious adverse events or discontinuations due to adverse events between anti-IL-1 therapeutics and placebo [N2-F1]. That is an important limitation because it means that safety concerns are not primarily driven by severe harms or treatment discontinuation, but rather by more frequent non-serious adverse events.

Safety concerns do limit broader use in knee OA, at least to some extent. The meta-analysis states that IL-1 inhibitors were associated with safety concerns and that IL-1 antibodies and IL-1 Ras were relatively safe options [N2-F1]. The critical synthesis also suggests that randomized clinical trials have been disappointing for knee OA and that safety may be a factor in negative results [N2-F2]. This implies that IL-1 inhibitors may not be broadly suitable for all knee OA patients because their safety profile is worse than placebo, even if the efficacy signal is not always strong.

Dose-related or injection-site safety patterns are not clearly established in the evidence provided. The meta-analysis does not report dose-related adverse events, and the excerpts do not give enough detail about injection-site reactions [N2-F1]. The background evidence refers to intra-articular anakinra and orthokin-like products, but the provided excerpts do not specify injection-site safety outcomes or dose-related toxicity [N5-F3; N6-R2; N6-R4]. Therefore, the evidence base is insufficient to conclude whether safety varies by dose or route.

Overall, the RCT evidence suggests that IL-1 inhibitors are not well tolerated compared with placebo, but the main safety concern appears to be more frequent adverse events rather than serious harms or discontinuation. This pattern limits their broader use in knee OA, even if the pain and function benefits are sometimes present [N2-F1; N2-F2].

The RCT evidence supports a cautious and conditional conclusion: IL-1 inhibitors may reduce pain and improve function in some knee OA patients, but the evidence base is incomplete, mixed, and not robust enough to support broad routine use. The most authoritative meta-analysis found that anti-IL-1 therapeutics were superior to placebo in pain relief and functional improvement, with a pain SMD of −0.38 and a functional SMD of −1.11, but also noted that the literature is incomplete and that inconsistent efficacy and safety make conclusions only partially supported [N2-F1]. The critical synthesis similarly says randomized clinical trials have read out negatively for knee OA, though it notes trends that may point to some benefit [N2-F2]. For synovitis-specific outcomes, the evidence is even more limited: inflammation and synovitis were mostly measured indirectly, and the provided evidence does not show a consistent or substantial synovitis-specific benefit in RCTs [N8].

## Supported conclusions
1. **Pain reduction is present but mixed.**  
   IL-1 inhibition appears to reduce OA-related pain and improve function in some trials, but the effect is not consistently large across all studies, and some RCTs did not show benefit [N2-F1; N2-F2]. The meta-analysis also found that IL-1 antibodies and IL-1 inhibitors were superior to placebo, while IL-1 Ras was not [N2-F1].  
   
2. **Synovitis is clinically relevant but not consistently targeted in trials.**  
   Synovial inflammation is present in OA joints, associated with radiographic and pain progression, and linked to more cartilage damage and pain worsening [N5-F3]. However, the RCT evidence provided does not show that IL-1 inhibitors consistently reduce synovitis or synovitis-specific endpoints; some trials using inflammatory mediators did not improve synovitis or OA progression [N8; N5-F3].  

3. **Safety concerns are real.**  
   IL-1 inhibitors are associated with an increased risk of adverse events compared with placebo, but the meta-analysis did not find a significant difference in serious adverse events or discontinuations due to adverse events [N2-F1]. This means the main safety issue is more frequent non-serious events than severe harm [N9].  

4. **Durable benefit is not established.**  
   The evidence provided does not support long-term durability beyond short-term follow-up; the meta-analysis does not report long-term data, and the background on synovitis and OA does not show sustained structural or symptomatic benefit from IL-1 inhibition [N7; N5-F3].  

## Gaps in evidence
The evidence base has several unresolved gaps:  
- **Synovitis-specific endpoints are underused or inconsistent.** The RCTs mostly rely on indirect measures such as pain, function, cartilage damage, and radiographic progression, rather than synovitis-specific outcomes [N8].  
- **Subgroup effects are not well characterized.** The meta-analysis identified some subgroup differences, but the excerpts do not specify which subgroups showed larger effects [N7].  
- **Dose and route effects are underreported.** The evidence does not provide sufficient detail on dose-related toxicity or injection-site safety [N9].  
- **Long-term safety and durability remain unclear.** The provided evidence does not address long-term harms or sustained benefit after short-term treatment [N7; N9].  
- **Comparisons with alternative therapies are limited.** The evidence base includes comparisons with placebo and NSAIDs, but less detail is available on head-to-head comparisons with other disease-modifying or symptomatic treatments [N7; N2-F1].  

## Implications for selecting patients and treatment sequences
The evidence suggests that IL-1 inhibition may be most appropriate for patients with active inflammation or synovitis, especially if pain and function are poorly controlled by standard care [N2-F2; N5-F3]. However, because the evidence is mixed and safety concerns exist, broader use should be limited to specific subgroups rather than routine knee OA. Treatment sequencing may involve IL-1 inhibitors earlier in patients with evidence of synovitis or inflammatory markers, but only after assessing baseline synovitis status and weighing risks against potential benefit [N7; N8; N9]. The evidence does not support a single “first-line” sequence for IL-1 inhibitors across all knee OA patients.

## Research priorities for better synovitis-targeted trials
The upstream evidence points to several research priorities:  
1. **Use synovitis-specific endpoints more consistently.** Trials should measure synovitis directly with imaging or synovitis-specific markers, rather than relying on indirect outcomes such as pain and function [N8].  
2. **Target patients with active synovitis.** Future trials should stratify by synovitis status and test whether IL-1 inhibition is more effective in patients with detectable synovitis or inflammation [N2-F2; N5-F3].

The meta-analysis does not report dose-related adverse events, and the excerpts do not give enough detail about injection-site reactions [N2-F1]. The background evidence refers to intra-articular anakinra and orthokin-like products, but the provided excerpts do not specify injection-site safety outcomes or dose-related toxicity [N5-F3; N6-R2; N6-R4]. Therefore, the evidence base is insufficient to conclude whether safety varies by dose or route.

### 4. What the evidence means for clinical practice and future research

Taken together, the evidence supports a cautious and conditional conclusion: IL-1 inhibitors may reduce pain and improve function in some knee OA patients, but the evidence base is incomplete, mixed, and not robust enough to support broad routine use. For patients with synovitis, the evidence is particularly limited because synovitis-specific endpoints were not consistently used and the RCTs mostly rely on indirect measures [N2-F1; N2-F2; N5-F3; N8].

#### Supported conclusions
- IL-1 inhibition may reduce pain and improve function in some patients, but the effect is not consistently large across all studies, and some RCTs did not show benefit [N2-F1; N2-F2].
- Synovial inflammation is clinically relevant, but the RCT evidence does not show a consistent or substantial synovitis-specific benefit [N5-F3; N8].
- IL-1 inhibitors are associated with an increased risk of adverse events, but the main safety issue is more frequent non-serious events than serious harms or discontinuation [N2-F1; N9].
- Durable benefit beyond short-term follow-up is not established [N7; N9].

#### Gaps in evidence
- Synovitis-specific endpoints are underused or inconsistent [N8].
- Subgroup effects are not well characterized [N7].
- Dose and route effects are underreported [N9].
- Long-term safety and durability remain unclear [N7; N9].
- Comparisons with alternative therapies are limited [N7; N2-F1].

#### Implications for selecting patients and treatment sequences
The evidence suggests that IL-1 inhibition may be most appropriate for patients with active inflammation or synovitis, especially if pain and function are poorly controlled by standard care [N2-F2; N5-F3]. However, because the evidence is mixed and safety concerns exist, broader use should be limited to specific subgroups rather than routine knee OA. Treatment sequencing may involve IL-1 inhibitors earlier in patients with evidence of synovitis or inflammatory markers, but only after assessing baseline synovitis status and weighing risks against potential benefit [N7; N8; N9]. The evidence does not support a single “first-line” sequence for IL-1 inhibitors across all knee OA patients.

#### Research priorities for better synovitis-targeted trials
The upstream evidence points to several research priorities:
1. Use synovitis-specific endpoints more consistently, such as imaging or synovitis-specific markers, rather than relying on indirect outcomes such as pain and function [N8].
2. Target patients with active synovitis and test whether IL-1 inhibition is more effective in those with detectable synovitis or inflammation [N2-F2; N5-F3].
3. Clarify the role of biomarkers to identify responders and improve patient selection [N4; N5-F3].
4. Improve trial design and dosing, including longer follow-up to assess durability and safety over time [N9].
5. Compare IL-1 inhibitors with other therapies, such as NSAIDs, disease-modifying agents, and synovitis-directed treatments [N7; N8].
6. Examine safety in larger and more diverse populations and over longer periods [N9].

### Bottom line for clinical practice
For knee OA patients with synovitis, the RCT evidence supports a cautious trial-of-the-needle approach: IL-1 inhibitors may help reduce pain and improve function in some patients, but the evidence is not strong enough to recommend routine use across all patients. Clinicians should prioritize patients with active synovitis, consider the safety profile, and use these agents only when the potential benefit is likely to outweigh the risks [N2-F1; N2-F2; N5-F3; N9]. Future research should focus on synovitis-specific endpoints, biomarker stratification, and durable safety data to better define the role of IL-1 inhibition in knee OA [N4; N8; N9].
